# Enterprise Data Governance Knowledge Guide for Database: codebase_community

## 1. Introduction
This Knowledge Guide serves as a comprehensive semantic layer for the database "codebase_community," providing authoritative guidance on data governance standards, core business entities, metric definitions, constraints, and exemplar use cases. It is designed to ensure consistency, accuracy, and clarity in data interpretation and usage across the enterprise.

## 2. Core Entities & Fields

### Users
- **Id**: Unique identifier for each user.
- **Display Name**: The name displayed publicly for the user.
- **Reputation**: Numerical value representing the user's standing within the community.
- **Creation Date**: Date when the user account was created.
- **Last Access Date**: Date of the user's most recent access.
- **Location**: Geographical location of the user.
- **Age**: Age of the user.
- **Views**: Number of times the user's profile has been viewed.
- **UpVotes/DownVotes**: Count of upvotes and downvotes received by the user.

### Posts
- **Id**: Unique identifier for each post.
- **Title**: The title of the post.
- **Body**: The main content of the post.
- **Score**: Rating score of the post.
- **View Count**: Number of times the post has been viewed.
- **Owner User Id**: Identifier for the user who created the post.
- **Creation Date**: Date when the post was created.
- **Tags**: Keywords associated with the post.
- **Answer Count**: Number of answers provided for the post.
- **Comment Count**: Number of comments on the post.
- **Favorite Count**: Number of times the post has been marked as a favorite.

### Comments
- **Id**: Unique identifier for each comment.
- **Post Id**: Identifier for the post associated with the comment.
- **Score**: Rating score of the comment.
- **Text**: Content of the comment.
- **Creation Date**: Date when the comment was created.
- **User Id**: Identifier for the user who posted the comment.

### Tags
- **Id**: Unique identifier for each tag.
- **Tag Name**: Name of the tag.
- **Count**: Number of posts associated with the tag.
- **Excerpt Post Id**: Identifier for the post that provides an excerpt for the tag.

### Votes
- **Id**: Unique identifier for each vote.
- **Post Id**: Identifier for the post that received the vote.
- **Vote Type Id**: Type of vote (e.g., upvote, downvote).
- **Creation Date**: Date when the vote was cast.
- **Bounty Amount**: Amount of bounty associated with the vote.

## 3. Metric Definitions

### Key Performance Indicators (KPIs)
- **User Engagement**: Calculated as the sum of views, upvotes, and downvotes for a user.
- **Post Popularity**: Determined by the view count and score of a post.
- **Community Growth**: Measured by the number of new users created within a specific time frame.
- **Content Quality**: Evaluated by the average score of posts and comments.
- **Tag Utilization**: Calculated as the count of posts associated with a specific tag.

### Calculation Logic
- **Average Score**: `AVG(Score)` for posts or comments.
- **Percentage of Elder Users**: `DIVIDE(COUNT(Id WHERE Age > 65), COUNT(Id)) * 100`.
- **Post-to-Vote Ratio**: `DIVIDE(Count(post.Id), Count(votes.Id))`.

## 4. Constraints & Conventions

### Filtering Criteria
- **Temporal Boundaries**: Use `YEAR(CreationDate)` for filtering by year.
- **Currency Formatting**: Ensure all monetary values are represented in USD.
- **Unit Conversion**: Age is represented in years; ensure consistency in calculations involving age.

### Common Conventions
- **Date Format**: Use 'YYYY-MM-DD' for all date-related queries.
- **Score Thresholds**: Define score thresholds for filtering posts and comments (e.g., Score > 5).

## 5. Exemplar Use Cases

### Example 1: User Reputation Comparison
**Metric**: Compare the reputation of users "Harlan" and "Jarrod Dixon."
**Explanation**: Identify the user with the highest reputation using `MAX(Reputation)` within the specified display names.

\n\n

\n\n

\n\n
\n\n

Some background on the problem:

\n\n

Say I have a family of models parametrized by $\\\\vec\\\\alpha = \\\\alpha_1, \\\\ldots \\\\alpha_n$. Say also that I have a set of $N$ data points and that I do model selection with k-fold cross-validation to choose the model that best generalizes the data.

\n\n

For model selection, I can do a grid search on the parameter space of $\\\\vec\\\\alpha$ running k-fold cross-validation for each $\\\\vec\\\\alpha$ candidate. I use matlab a lot to fit functions to datasets. I then need to determine some kind of error estimate on the fitted parameters.

\n\n

Say I have a dataset of $N$ points which is given by the points $(x_i,y_i),\\\\ i=1,\\\\ldots,N$. I need to fit a function $f(x,P)$ where $P$ is the parameter matrix

\n\n

$$P = \\\\left[\\\\begin{array}{cc} a_1\\\\\\\\ a_2\\\\\\\\\\\\vdots\\\\\\\\a_k\\\\end{array}\\\\right]$$

\n\n

where $k$ is the number of parameters to be fitted. I use the root-mean-squared method to find estimates for parameters $a_1,\\\\ldots,a_k$. I build an error function:

\n\n

$$\\\\varepsilon(P,x,y)= \\\\frac{1}{N}\\\\left(\\\\sum\\\\limits_{i=1}^N (f(x,P)-y)^2\\\\right)^{\\\\frac{1}{2}}$$

\n\n

and then use the matlab function fminsearch to get the minimum of this function by optimizing $P$. (I know there are better matlab functions, but bare with me).

\n\n

To get the estimates I calculate the Jacobian matrix $J_f$:

\n\n

$$J_f = \\\\left[\\\\begin{array}{c}\\\\frac{\\\\partial f}{\\\\partial a_1}(P',x) \\\\\\\\ \\\\frac{\\\\partial f}{\\\\partial a_2}(P',x)\\\\\\\\ \\\\vdots\\\\end{array}\\\\right]$$

\n\n

where $P'$ denotes the fitted parameter matrix (best values to minimize the error function $\\\\varepsilon$). I also calculate the variance on the residuals:

\n\n

$$ \\\\sigma_r = \\\\frac{1}{N-k}\\\\sum\\\\limits_{i=1}^N r_i^2$$

\n\n

with

\n\n

$$ r_i = y_i - f(P',x_i), $$

\n\n

the residuals. I can get the covariance matrix now:

\n\n

$$ \\\\operatorname{cov}(P) = \\\\sigma_r(J_f^TJ_f)^{-1} $$

\n\n

where the upper script $T$ stands for transposing and upper script $-1$ stands for the inverse matrix. TO get the error estimates I then need to get the point-wise square root of the covariance matrix:

\n\n

$$s_P = \\\\left[ \\\\begin{array}{c} s_{a_1} \\\\\\\\ s_{a_2} \\\\\\\\ \\\\vdots \\\\end{array}\\\\right] = \\\\sqrt{\\\\operatorname{cov}(P)}$$

\n\n

while $f'$ is:

I have access to a very large dataset. The data is from MEG recordings of people listening to musical excerpts, from one of four genres. The data is as follows:

\n\n
    \n
  • 6 Subjects
    • \n
  • 3 Experimental repetitions (epochs)
    • \n
  • 120 Trials per epoch
    • \n
  • 8 seconds of data per trial at 500Hz (=4000 samples) from 275 MEG channels
    • \n
\n\n

So each \"example\" here is a matrix of size [4000x275], and there are 2160 of such examples, and that's before any feature extraction. The goal is to predict genre based on the brain signal (4-class classification).

\n\n

Clearly there are some challenging issues here, namely:

\n\n
    \n
  1. The dataset does not fit in memory
    2. \n
  2. There will be strong temporal correlations in the data, and the inter-subject variation will be huge. As a result it's not obvious how to split the data
    3. \n
  3. The signal-to-noise ratio is very low
    4. \n
  4. It's not obvious what the correct features for a classifier would be
    5. \n
\n\n

Taking these in turn:

\n\n
    \n

  1. There are various things one can do. Firstly we can safely downsample from 500Hz to ~200Hz, as even taking the Nyquist limit into account, brain activity doesn't really occur at over 100Hz. We could also subsample from the the set of channels (e.g. centre over auditory areas) but we'd rather not do this a-priori, as there may be activity in other areas (frontal etc) that could be of interest. We can probably also drop a portion of the time window. Perhaps only the first 2s is important for the task? It's not really known. Of course everyone will shout \"Dimensionality reduction!\", but that's not trivial either. Firstly, we'd have to be very careful about our train/test splits (see 2.) and it's also not obvious whether to do this before or after feature generation. Secondly, other than expensive cross-validation, or painstaking visual inspection, there's no obvious way to select either the appropriate method or the appropriate number of dimensions. We could of course just use e.g. PCA, ICA, or random projections and hope for the best ....

    2. \n

  2. This is tricky. If we have successive samples in the training set we are likely to overfit the training set, whereas if we have successive samples split into to the train and test sets we're likely to underfit the training set, but could still overfit the testing set. There seem to be various options here:

    \n\n
      \n
    • Single Subject Classification. Take each individual subject on their own, and split according to epochs. This should be the easiest task, as we're not trying to predict across brains. Within this one could use the two remain epochs for cross-validation. For completeness one should rotate all combinations. We would simply report the average accuracy over all subjects. Of course we would not expect these models to generalise well at all.
      • \n
    • Within subjects classification. Take all of the subjects together, and split according to epochs. This may in fact be the easiest task, as we will have seen all of the subjects in training. However we probably wouldn't expect the models to generalise well to new subjects. Within this one could use the two remain epochs for cross-validation. For completeness one should rotate all combinations.
      • \n
    • Between subjects classification. Also known as \"leave-one-out\", where a single subject is taken as test data, and the rest are used for training. We would then rotate through all subjects. Cross-validation would then be performed over subjects. We would expect this to be a much more difficult task, as we are trying to predict on a \"new brain\" each time. Here we would expect the models to generalise well to the larger population, although there is an issue of test-retest reliability (i.e. how much overfitting is caused by temporal correlations).
      • \n
    3. \n

  3. This is a classical \"needle in a haystack\" problem - the actual signal relating to the recognition of musical genre, or any genre-specific processing, is likely to be minuscule compared to the \"soup\" of activity in the brain. There are also notable artefacts which can only be partially removed (mainly related to movement). Any features that we derive from the data, and any ways in which the data is treated, should avoid destroying part of the signal of interest.

    4. \n

  4. Here one could imagine doing various things. The first would be to simply use the raw data (concatenated into a vector) as the feature vector. I'm not sure how fruitful that is though - I think these vectors would probably be essentially uniformly random. This is then really a signal processing question, but there are some general guidelines one can follow. One is to do standard Fourier Analysis over a sliding window, from where the components can be split into distinct frequency bands (alpha/beta/gamma etc), and statistics of these (mean, std. deviation) can be used as features. Or one could use Wavelets, Hilbert Transforms, or even attempt to look for chaotic attractors. Of course then we have the choice of kernels (linear, polynomial, RBF etc) which multiplies up the number of permutations. Perhaps the best thing to do here is generate as many different feature sets as possible, and then use MKL or boosting methods to combine them together.

    5. \n
\n\n

How would you approach this kind of dataset (if not this one specifically)? Is there anything I've missed along the way? What is the most likely strategy to succeed, without spending endless amounts of researcher time and computational resources?

    \n

As some of you may now, various statistical tests are used in the task of finding collocations in given text(either a single document or corpus of texts). Chi-square, t-test, likelihood ratio(with binomial distribution assumed). These tests are used to check if two words occur together significantly more often that apart from each other, that's how the strenth of collocation is measured.

\n\n

A-a-anyway, one good thing to do is put your hands onto a large corpus of texts and save contingency tables(or just frequencies, really) of all the bigrams(two words) and unigrams(one word, obviously) from this corpus. We call this information background.

\n\n

Little introduction for you there, now to the main part:\nwhen you receive a text(call it foreground), you extract all bigrams from it and have to decide whether this is a collocation or just some pair of words, like \"of the\" or \"and yes\", which do not bear any meaning and not at all important in this particular text.

\n\n

Now, to the question: when you stumble upon a bigram that has in fact been seen in background, it means that both unigrams it consists of can be found in background too, all frequencies are in place, everything else is a piece of cake.

\n\n

But what if this bigram has never occurred before? The only place we can find it in is our foreground, but there's not enough information to infer the distribution and collocation strength. I mean, you can apply any of these statistical tests to foreground contingency table, but it won't be the same, you know? Not that reliable, I suppose.

\n\n

So, at last, to the question itself, all two parts of it:

\n\n

1) What to do with bigrams that have never occurred in background corpus(and both unigrams are not there either, just two words we haven't seen before)

\n\n

2) What to do with bigrams only one part of which has occurred in background corpus?

\n\n

3) What to do with bigrams that have never occured in background corpus, but both words from it are present in background corpus?

\n\n

How to make it smooth, so some scores of collocation strength can be created for all these cases and were at least a little reliable.

\n\n

Thank you in advance, kick this question to whatever site is appropriate if I've misunderstood the purpose of this particular part of stackexchange.

There is no mechanical problem with your model, but you need to\n consider carefully whether any of the reported standard errors mean\n anything. The theory that justifies the standard error calculation is\n asymptotic in the number of clusters, and we have just established\n that you are estimating at least as many parameters as you have\n clusters.

\n \n

That concern aside, the model test statistic issue is that you cannot\n simultaneously test that all coefficients are zero because there is\n not enough information. You could test a subset, but not all, and so\n Stata refuses to report the overall model test statistic.

\n \n

Here note the degrees of freedom reported for the chi2 or F. You\n might see chi2(6) or F(6, 5). Reading the book \"Microeconometrics using Stata\", the author clearly indicates that the xtreg command, with the vce(cluster id) option for calculating robust errors, is mostly appropriate for short panels.

However, we have tested, and our errors do not show an AR(1) pattern (xtserial test). The xtregar command has the option rhof(#), where # indicates the desired rho value (AR(rho)).

Although some folds may yield the same tree, it's very likely that the majority of folds will yield a different decision tree, in other words a different pattern.\nI would like to ask the following questions :

\n\n
    \n

  1. If each fold reports a different decision tree but gives good classification accuracy, does this mean there is no consistent pattern ? Off course there may be a lot of ways to divide a dataset, not all of them covered by a k-fold validation.

    2. \n

  2. Cross-validation aims to assess the performance of a classifier. But when each fold yields a completely different decision tree, does it make sense to assess the performance only by looking at the classification accuracy AUC, TP/FP rates ?
